w: Founded in 1817 in Lwow by Count Jozef Maksymilian Ossolinski, this archive and publishing house survived empire, war and forced relocation before landing in Wroclaw in 1947. Its imprint is the oldest continuously running in the Polish language, and its collection is Poland's second-largest after Krakow's.
s: Poland's exiled national archive, reborn in Wroclaw
_facts: Founded 1817 in Lwow (now Lviv) by Count Jozef Maksymilian Ossolinski, a Polish nobleman
Relocated to Wroclaw in 1947; second largest institution of its kind in Poland after the Jagiellonian Library
Its publishing arm is the oldest continuous imprint in Polish since the early 19th century

w: Opened in 1865 as the Breslau Zoological Garden, this is Poland's oldest zoo -- shut down and battered across two world wars, then rebuilt from the ground up after 1945. Today it holds roughly 10,500 animals across 1,132 species, making it the country's largest zoo and, by species count, the third-largest on Earth.
s: Poland's oldest zoo, rebuilt twice from ruin
_facts: Opened 1865 as the Breslau Zoological Garden; oldest zoo in Poland
Shut down during the World Wars, rebuilt and reopened in 1948
About 10,500 animals across roughly 1,132 species; largest zoo in Poland by species, third-largest worldwide
Most visited zoo in Poland, fifth most visited in Europe

w: Established in 1947 and inaugurated the following year, this branch of Poland's National Museum grew out of a city still rebuilding from ruin into a keeper of one of the country's largest contemporary art collections. Its galleries carry Silesia's shifting borders as much as its art history.
s: A postwar museum holding one of Poland's biggest art troves
_facts: Established 28 March 1947, officially inaugurated 11 July 1948
One of Poland's main National Museum branches
Holds one of the largest collections of contemporary art in Poland

w: In 1929, Weimar-era Breslau's Werkbund architects threw up 32 experimental buildings in three months near Scheitniger Park -- a crash course in functionalist housing, wooden kindergarten included. Hans Scharoun's block for singles and couples still stands, now a hotel, and the estate carries a European Heritage Label.
s: A functionalist housing experiment built in three months
_facts: 1929 building exhibition in Breslau (now Wroclaw), organised by the Silesian Deutsche Werkbund
32 building types built within three months near Scheitniger Park
Hans Scharoun's house for singles and young couples survives, now used as a hotel
The area received the European Heritage Label from the European Commission

w: Nuns of the Order of Saint Clare bleached linen on this Oder islet for centuries before it took their name. WWII bombardment leveled most of its houses, but the medieval St. Clare's Mills survived -- until the city dynamited them in 1975 by mayoral order, a move that drew outrage and left the island empty for years.
s: A river island the city dynamited in 1975
_facts: Small islet on the Oder within the Wroclaw Old Town, formerly called Vorderbleiche
Owned by the Order of Saint Clare from the Middle Ages until the early 18th century, used for bleaching linen
Heavily bombarded in WWII; the surviving 13th-century St. Clare's Mills were demolished by city order in 1975, sparking protest

w: Tucked into an old mercantile building on Theatre Square, next to the public baths, this puppet theatre has staged marionette shows in the city for generations -- a small, storied stage hiding inside a repurposed trading hall.
s: Marionettes on stage in a former trading hall
_facts: Also known as Teatr Lalek; located on Theatre Square
Housed in an old mercantile building next to the Old Town Garden and public baths

w: Founded in 1872 under German ownership as Brauerei Pfeifferhof, it was renamed Piast in 1945 to honour Poland's first royal dynasty, staffed by Polish brewmasters uprooted from Lwow when the border shifted. Carlsberg bought the works in 2001 and shut the taps for good in 2004, ending over a century of brewing here.
s: A brewery renamed for a dynasty, closed by Carlsberg
_facts: Founded 1872 by Carl Scholtz as Brauerei Pfeifferhof; renamed Piast Brewery in 1945
Postwar production run by Polish brewmasters relocated from Lwow
Bought by Carlsberg Polska in 2001; brewing terminated in 2004
